title: Ecological Pyramids, Keystone Species and Biomagnification

cards.b:
Pyramids, keystone species and biomagnification are asked almost every other year. They are short concepts, so options are tricky and one wrong word costs the mark.

They also power Mains answers on pollution (DDT, mercury), invasive species and wildlife management. Learn the exact definitions once and reuse them.

Charles Elton (1927) introduced the pyramid idea. There are three kinds.

  • Pyramid of number: counts of organisms. Can be upright or inverted.
  • Pyramid of biomass: dry weight per area. Inverted in the sea.
  • Pyramid of energy: energy per area per time. Always upright, never inverted.

Energy is lost as heat at each step, so the energy pyramid cannot flip.

In a tree ecosystem one big tree supports thousands of insects, so the number pyramid is inverted. A parasitic food chain (tree, birds, lice) is also inverted in numbers.

In a pond or ocean the producers are tiny phytoplankton that reproduce fast. At any moment their standing biomass is less than that of zooplankton and fish, so the biomass pyramid is inverted. But their energy turnover is huge, so the energy pyramid stays upright.

The term comes from Robert Paine (1969), who removed the starfish Pisaster from a rocky shore in Washington. Mussels took over and diversity fell.

A keystone species has an effect far larger than its numbers. Examples: sea otters (they control sea urchins and so protect kelp), African elephants, tigers as top predators, and figs in tropical forests. An umbrella species (tiger, elephant) protects many others when its habitat is protected. A flagship species is chosen to raise public support. An indicator species shows habitat health, such as lichens for air quality.

Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a substance inside one organism. Biomagnification is its rise in concentration at each higher trophic level. It happens for substances that are persistent and fat-soluble, so they are not excreted.

DDT is the classic case. Rachel Carson wrote Silent Spring (1962) on it. DDT thinned the eggshells of eagles and pelicans. Mercury in fish caused Minamata disease in Japan (1956). Cadmium caused Itai-itai disease.

Eutrophication is nutrient over-enrichment of water. It is not biomagnification.

Ecological efficiency is the share of energy passed up a trophic level, about 10 percent (Lindeman 1942).

Gross primary productivity is total energy fixed by producers. Net primary productivity is GPP minus respiration loss. NPP is what is available to consumers.

Standing crop is the mass of living matter at a point in time. Standing state is the amount of nutrients in soil.

cards.h: Is the keystone idea too neat?
cards.b:
Critics say few species are true keystones. A species can be keystone in one place and ordinary in another. Rewilding projects, such as wolves in Yellowstone (1995), are praised for trophic cascades, but scientists still argue about how large the effect was.

Conservation money is limited. Protecting umbrella species is efficient, but it may leave small, unattractive endemic species without cover.

The tiger is India's umbrella species, and Project Tiger (1973) protects whole forests with it. The Asian elephant is a keystone seed disperser.

The vulture crash is a lesson in chains. Livestock treated with diclofenac left toxic carcasses. White-backed, long-billed and slender-billed vultures fell by over 95 percent in the 1990s. India banned veterinary diclofenac in 2006. Dead cattle rotted, and feral dogs and rabies cases increased.

Sundarbans, Chilika and the Ganga show DDT and heavy-metal traces in fish.

Remember the one-line rule. Number and biomass pyramids can be inverted. The energy pyramid cannot.

A grassland has an upright number pyramid. A forest tree has an inverted one. A sea has an inverted biomass pyramid. All three have upright energy pyramids. Questions often give an example and ask which pyramid is inverted. Match the example to the type.

Prelims-style: "Which pyramid is always upright?" (energy). "Who proposed the keystone concept?" (Paine, 1969). "Biomagnification is caused by substances that are persistent and fat-soluble."

Mains-style: "How can the loss of a keystone species threaten an ecosystem? Give Indian examples." Structure: define; Paine's starfish; effect on trophic cascade; Indian cases (vultures, elephants, tiger); policy response; conclusion.

quiz.q: Who introduced the concept of ecological pyramids in 1927?
quiz.w: Elton described the pyramid of numbers; Lindeman gave the ten percent law (1942).
Energy is lost as heat at every step, so the energy pyramid cannot invert.

quiz.q: The pyramid of biomass in a pond is usually:
quiz.w: Tiny, fast-breeding phytoplankton have less standing biomass than the animals that feed on them.

quiz.q: The keystone species idea was introduced by:
quiz.w: Paine worked with the starfish Pisaster.

quiz.q: Biomagnification needs a substance that is:
quiz.w: Such substances are stored in fat and are not broken down.

quiz.q: Minamata disease in Japan was caused by:
quiz.w: Cadmium caused Itai-itai; mercury caused Minamata.

quiz.q: Which Indian drug ban in 2006 was linked to vulture decline?
quiz.w: Diclofenac in cattle carcasses poisoned vultures.

quiz.q: A species whose protection also covers many others in its habitat is called:
quiz.w: Tiger and elephant are common umbrella species.
NPP is what remains for consumers.

quiz.q: Which book by Rachel Carson raised alarm about DDT?
